attribution: Acid and deacidification figures are the standard oenological approximations: 1 g/L of a monoprotic addition moves titratable acidity by roughly 1 g/L, expressed as tartaric. Real musts are buffered, so the pH change for a given TA change varies with potassium and the starting acid profile — always measure rather than assuming. Compiled from OIV oenological practice and standard winemaking references.

additives.name: Tartaric Acid
additives.description: The principal grape acid and the only common wine acid that resists metabolism by lactic bacteria. Adding 1 g/L raises titratable acidity by about 1 g/L and lowers pH, though how far depends on the must's buffering.
additives.usageNotes: The default acidulant for grape wine. Add before fermentation so the potassium bitartrate has time to precipitate out during cold stabilisation.
additives.cautions: Some of what you add will drop out as tartrate crystals, so the measured TA after cold stabilisation will be lower than the arithmetic predicts.

additives.name: Malic Acid
additives.description: The sharp green-apple acid of apples, stone fruit and unripe grapes. Tastes harsher than tartaric at the same titratable acidity.
additives.usageNotes: The natural acid of cider and most fruit. Use where a crisp, appley acidity is wanted.
additives.cautions: Lactic bacteria convert malic to lactic acid, softening the wine and releasing CO2 — a bottled wine with residual malic can referment.

additives.name: Citric Acid
additives.description: The citrus acid. Bright and immediate on the palate but the least stable of the three in wine.
additives.usageNotes: Common in fruit wines and meads, where its flavour fits. Also chelates iron and copper.
additives.cautions: Lactic bacteria metabolise citric acid to diacetyl and acetic acid — do not use it in a wine that will undergo malolactic conversion.

additives.name: Lactic Acid
additives.description: The softest-tasting of the common acids. Usually sold as an 88% solution rather than a powder.
additives.usageNotes: The standard mash pH adjustment in brewing, and a gentle finishing acid elsewhere.
additives.cautions: At 88% strength, 1 mL weighs about 1.2 g and delivers roughly 1.05 g of acid — dose by weight, not volume.

additives.name: Phosphoric Acid
additives.description: A strong mineral acid that shifts pH sharply with very little flavour contribution.
additives.usageNotes: Preferred for mash and sparge water adjustment where any acid flavour would be unwelcome.
additives.cautions: Far stronger than the organic acids — a small overshoot is hard to undo. Add in small increments and remeasure.

additives.name: Acid Blend
additives.description: A packaged mixture, usually tartaric, malic and citric in roughly equal parts.
additives.usageNotes: Convenient for country wines where no single varietal acid profile is being targeted.
additives.cautions: The citric fraction makes it a poor choice ahead of malolactic conversion.

additives.name: Tannic Acid
additives.description: A hydrolysable tannin preparation, sold as an acid but functioning as an astringency addition.
additives.usageNotes: Use the purpose-made oenological tannins below in preference — they are better characterised.
additives.cautions: Easy to overdose into harsh astringency.

additives.name: Potassium Bicarbonate
additives.description: The standard wine deacidifier: roughly 1 g/L drops titratable acidity by about 1 g/L, precipitating the acid as potassium bitartrate.
additives.usageNotes: Add after fermentation, then cold stabilise so the tartrate actually drops out. Works on tartaric acid, not malic.
additives.cautions: Do not exceed about 3 g/L — beyond that the wine turns salty and flat, and the pH rise brings microbial risk. Effect only completes after cold stabilisation.

additives.name: Calcium Carbonate
additives.description: A faster and cheaper deacidifier than potassium bicarbonate, but it leaves calcium behind.
additives.usageNotes: Use where a large acid reduction is needed and the wine will be given months to throw its calcium tartrate.
additives.cautions: Calcium tartrate precipitates slowly and unpredictably — sometimes in the bottle. Leaves a chalky character if overdone.

additives.name: Potassium Carbonate
additives.description: A stronger relative of potassium bicarbonate, slightly more effective per gram.
additives.usageNotes: Same handling as potassium bicarbonate; less commonly stocked.
additives.cautions: Raises pH faster than bicarbonate — overshoot is easier.
